ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: In the circuit shown in Figure A, it is known that the resistance values of resistor R and self-induction coil L are both very small, and are smaller than the resistance of bulb A; after closing S to make the circuit reach stability and then opening S, how will the brightness of bulb A change?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In Figure A, the wires on the left and right sides form two common nodes; the upper branch goes from the left node successively through bulb A and self-induction coil L to the right node; the middle branch has resistor R connected between the left and right nodes; the lower branch has power supply E and switch S, and when the switch is closed the power supply is connected in, while when it is opened the lower branch is cut off. Reasoning: After S is closed and stability is reached, in the DC steady state the self-induction coil L is equivalent to a resistor with a very small resistance value. In the upper branch, bulb A and L are connected in series, so there is a steady current in bulb A and it lights up. At the instant S is opened, the power-supply branch is opened, but the current in L cannot change abruptly; since A and L are connected in series, the current maintained by L is also the original upper-branch current of bulb A, and it cannot suddenly increase, nor can it immediately become zero. After opening, A and L in the upper branch and R in the middle branch can still form a closed freewheeling loop, and the current gradually decays through R. The brightness of the bulb is determined by the current through it, so bulb A gradually weakens starting from its original brightness, and finally goes out.
